text: Why is `If` the only node type that does not evaluate all of its children?
choices: Because a conditional is a statement rather than an expression, and statements have no value.
Because the test's value is not known until run time, unlike an operator's operands.
Because evaluating the unused branch would be a performance cost the interpreter cannot afford.
Because evaluating both branches would call the recursive branch even at the base case, so no recursion could ever terminate.
explanation: `if n < 2 then 1 else n * fact(n - 1)` would call `fact` at every level including the base case. Conditional evaluation is not an optimization; it is the thing that makes recursion possible. It is also why `&&` and `||` short-circuit in Java and why they cannot be ordinary methods — a method's arguments are evaluated before the call, and short-circuiting requires not evaluating one.
